ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In figure (i) there is a 100 V DC power supply, an ideal switch S, a diode connected to the lower bus, and the diode voltage is labeled v_D; this node is then connected through an inductor labeled 1 mH to the large capacitor C and the load on the right side. In figure (ii), the v_D waveform, within each 0.10 ms period, is 100 V for the first 0.05 ms and 0 V for the latter 0.05 ms, and repeats in this way. Reasoning: Regard v_D as the voltage of the left end of the inductor relative to the lower bus. In steady state, the average voltage of the inductor is zero, and the capacitor voltage is approximately constant, so the output/capacitor voltage equals the average value of v_D: V_C = 100 × (0.05/0.10) = 50 V. When v_D is 100 V, the inductor voltage v_L = 100 - 50 = 50 V, lasting 0.05 ms; when v_D is 0 V, v_L = 0 - 50 = -50 V, lasting 0.05 ms. The change amount of the inductor current during the high-level interval is Δi = (v_L/L)Δt = (50/1 mH)(0.05 ms) = 2.5 A. Therefore the peak-to-peak ripple of the inductor current is 2.5 A.

method.method_draft: First identify v_D as the voltage at the left side of the inductor relative to the lower rail. From the waveform, its average over one 0.10 ms period is (100 V)(0.05/0.10)=50 V, so the constant capacitor/output voltage must be 50 V in steady state. Therefore, during the high interval, v_L = 100−50 = 50 V for 0.05 ms; during the low interval, v_L = 0−50 = −50 V for 0.05 ms. Compute the current rise over the high interval: Δi = (50 V / 1 mH)(0.05 ms) = 2.5 A, which is the peak-to-peak ripple.

method.method_draft: Treat the circuit as an ideal buck chopper because the switch connects the 100 V source to the inductor node and the diode provides the freewheel path.
